body.p: Claims 1-27 are pending in the application, and claims 16-21 are withdrawn from consideration.
Claims1-15 and 22-27 are rejected.

Claims 1, 4-9, 12,14,15,19, 21, 26 and 27 are amended above, and claims 28 and 29 are newly added. Support is provided by the originally filed specification, claims, and drawings. No new matter has been added.

Applicant reserves the right to reassert any of the claims cancelled or the original or previous claim scope of any claim amended, during the prosecution of this application, in this continuing application.
In view of the above, favorable consideration is respectfully requested.
Claims 8, 12, and 15 are objected to on page 4 of the Office Action. The claims are amended above in response thereto.
Claim 26 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph on page 5 of the Office Action. Claim 26 is amended above in response thereto.
Claims 4-7, 14, 15, and 26 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph on page 6 of the Office Action.
The claims are amended above in response thereto.
A. Claims 1-8, 11-15, 22-25, and 27 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C.
102(b) as being anticipated by Wang et al. ("Wang", US 2011/0302694) on
page 8 of theOffice Action.
The Office Action asserts that claims 1-8, 11-15, 22-25, and 27 are anticipated by Wang.
This rejection is respectfully traversed.

Wang discloses a glove 102 having a flexible sensor 104. The flexible sensor is operationally coupled to a light detector 106, a light source 108, and a second light detector 110. A wrist cuff 112 includes a control panel 114, which may house the operational circuitry and one or more power supplies for the light source 108 and the light detectors 106 and 110. A cable 116 operationally couples the control panel 114 to a data acquisition module 118. The data acquisition module 118 is operationally coupled to a graphical display and control module 120.

It is noted that in Wang, the glove 102 and wrist cuff 112 are separate components, and wrist cuff 112 is not part of the glove, as shown in FIG. 1. Thus, in Wang the glove 102 does not comprise a microprocessor.

Specifically, Wang discloses that the "wrist cuff 112 includes circuitry for driving the light source 106, collecting signals from the light detectors 108 and 110, amplifying the signal (amplifier 604), converting analog to digital, indicating conditions on the wrist cuff 112, transmitting the data wirelessly to the control and display unit 620, and housing a rechargeable battery" (see paragraphs [0138] and [0139]).

Wang does not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a microcontroller secured to the glove." Further, Wang does not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a glove, comprising: at least one layer of material; one or more pressure sensors secured to and located secured to and located adjacent to a side edge of the glove, the one or more pressure sensors configured for detecting pressure applied by a user's

hand wearing the glove onto a vertebra or soft tissue of an individual, and a microcontroller secured to and located on the glove, the microcontroller electrically connected to the one or more pressure sensors, the microcontroller receiving electrical signal inputs from the one or more sensors and generating an output signal."

In view of the above, it is submitted that Wang does not teach each and every element of the claims as required for anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102. Thus, the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw this rejection.
B. Claims 1-15, 22-25, and 27 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as
being anticipated by Montgomery (US 2012/018543) on page 9 of the
Office Action.
The Office Action asserts that claims 1-15 are anticipated by Montgomery.
This rejection is respectfully traversed.
Montgomery discloses a glove device 10 having multiple force sensors 34, a component 36 that is in communication with each of the forces sensors 34, and a motion sensor 40, as shown in FIGS. 1 and 2.

The component 36 comprises a digital signal processor that receives signals from the force sensors 34 and forwards them on to another device, such as a computer. In other embodiments, the component 36 comprises one or more pressure transducers that sense the pressure of the fluid within the forces sensors 34.

Montgomery does not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a microcontroller secured to the glove." Further, Wang does not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a glove, comprising: at least one layer of material; one or more pressure sensors secured to and located adjacent to a side edge of the glove, the one or more pressure sensors configured for detecting pressure applied by a user's hand wearing the glove onto a vertebra or soft tissue of an individual, and a microcontroller secured to and located on the glove, the microcontroller electrically connected to the one or more pressure sensors, the microcontroller receiving electrical signal inputs from the one or more sensors and generating an output signal."

In view of the above, it is submitted that Montgomery does not teach each and every element of the claims as required for anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102. Thus, the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw this rejection.
A. Claim 9 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable
over Wang in view of Montgomery on page 16 of the Office Action.
The Office Action asserts that "[I]t would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to mount the control panel 114 of Wang between

adjacent layers of the glove (pages 4 and 7 of Montgomery. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention to mount the control panel 114 of Wang between adjacent layers of Montgomery since (1) it can protect the control panel 114 and/or (2) it is a simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results."
Wang and Montgomery are discussed in detail above, which discussions are incorporated herein by reference.

Again, Wang and Montgomery each do not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a microcontroller secured to the glove." Further, Wang does not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a glove, comprising: at least one layer of material; one or more pressure sensors secured to and located adjacent to a side edge of the glove, the one or more pressure sensors configured for detecting pressure applied by a user's

hand wearing the glove onto a vertebra or soft tissue of an individual, and a microcontroller secured to and located on the glove, the microcontroller electrically connected to the one or more pressure sensors, the microcontroller receiving electrical signal inputs from the one or more sensors and generating an output signal."
Thus, factually Wang and/or Montgomery cannot teach or suggest the claimed subject matter.

In view of above, nothing in Wang and Montgomery, taken alone or in combination, renders the subject matter of the claims obvious within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 103. Accordingly, the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw this rejection.
B. Claim 10 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable
over Wang on page 16 of the Office Action.

The Office Action asserts that "[I]t would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to substitute the sensors of FIGS. 1-2 and paragraph [0111] of Wang with the sensor of FIG. 31 and paragraph [0228] of Wang, since it is a simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results."
Wang is discussed in detail above, which discussion is incorporated herein by reference.

Again, Wang does not disclose the base claimed subject matter, including ""a microcontroller secured to the glove." Further, Wang does not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a glove, comprising: at least one layer of material; one or more pressure sensors secured to and located adjacent to a side edge of the glove, the one or more pressure sensors configured for detecting pressure applied by a user's hand wearing the glove onto a vertebra or soft tissue of an individual, and a microcontroller secured to and located on the glove, the microcontroller electrically connected to the one or more pressure sensors, the microcontroller receiving electrical signal inputs from the one or more sensors and generating an output signal."
Thus, factually Wang cannot teach or suggest the claimed subject matter.
In view of above, nothing in Wang renders the subject matter of the claims obvious within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 103. Accordingly, the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw this rejection.
C. Claim 26 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable
over Wang in view of Bishara (US 2014/0052026) on page 17 of the Office
Action.

The Office Action asserts that "[I]t would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to select the number and location of the sensors so as to obtain the desired preferences of the designer and/or user and the desired location of the pressure measurements. Using the locations indicated in FIG. 2A of Wang, the location of the sensors in the thumb and index finger only would have been obvious."
Wang is discussed in detail above, which discussion is incorporated herein by reference.
Bishara is cited only for the purpose of disclosing "that it is known to provide sleeves to only those sensors located in the finger and thumb sleeves (FIGS. 3A-3B of Bishara).

Wang and Bishara both do not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a microcontroller secured to the glove." Further, Wang does not disclose the claimed subject matter, including "a glove, comprising: at least one layer of material; one or more pressure sensors secured to and located adjacent to a side edge of the glove, the one or more pressure sensors configured for detecting pressure applied by a user's hand wearing the glove onto a vertebra or soft tissue of an individual, and a microcontroller secured to and located on the glove, the microcontroller electrically connected to the one or more pressure sensors, the microcontroller receiving electrical signal inputs from the one or more sensors and generating an output signal."
Thus, factually Wang and Bishara cannot teach or suggest the claimed subject matter.

In view of above, nothing in Wang and Bishara, alone or in combination, renders the subject matter of the claims obvious within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 103. Accordingly, the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw this rejection.
